title: Foreign Keys and One-to-Many Relationships
summary: Understand how a foreign key links a child table to a parent table, what referential integrity prevents, and how to identify the one side and the many side of a 1:M relationship.

steps.title: Linking Orders Back to the Right Customer
steps.lede: Every order belongs to some customer. The orders table needs a column that points back to the exact customer row — and a rule that keeps that pointer from dangling.

blocks.text: Every order in the orders table belongs to some customer. The orders table needs a way to point back to the exact customer row it belongs to, and to make sure that pointer is never left dangling.

blocks.title: Foreign key link: orders.customer_id → customers.customer_id
blocks.alt_text: Two table boxes: customers (customer_id PK, name, city) and orders (order_id PK, customer_id FK, delivery_minutes). An arrow runs from orders.customer_id to customers.customer_id. A third box shows an order row with customer_id = 99 whose arrow has no target in customers — an orphan record.

blocks.text: A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or group of columns) of one table must match values appearing in some row of another, referenced table. orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers.customer_id — every customer_id value in orders must match an actual customer_id already in customers.

A null foreign key value satisfies referential integrity — an order with no customer_id at all doesn't violate the constraint. But a non-null value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table. A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record; referential integrity is what prevents these.

steps.title: Foreign Keys Build the Parent-Child Link
steps.lede: See how a foreign key value must already exist in the parent table, or the database refuses the insert.

segments.label: A foreign key value must already exist in the parent table, or the insert is refused
segments.summary: Describes a foreign key as the column that builds a parent-child relationship between tables, using an orders table whose customer ID column points to the customer ID in the customers table. A new order for customer ID 101 is allowed only if 101 already exists in customers; otherwise the database refuses it, which is what referential integrity means. It ends with the rule that the column being referenced must be a primary key or a unique key.

blocks.group_title: Foreign keys build the parent-child link

bridge.before: Watch for the parent-child idea: the orders column can only hold values that already exist in customers.
bridge.after: The clip does not use the term orphan record and does not say a foreign key may be empty (NULL). Both are in the text above.

steps.title: What Breaks Referential Integrity?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of what creates an orphan record.

public.prompt: An orders row has customer_id = 99, but no row in the customers table has customer_id = 99. What is this row called, and what rule does it break?

options.text: An orphan record — it breaks referential integrity because the foreign key value has no matching primary key in the referenced table
A valid row — a null or unmatched foreign key is always acceptable
A duplicate record — it breaks the uniqueness requirement of the primary key
An entity integrity violation — the primary key of the orders table is null

opt_orphan.message: Correct. A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record, and referential integrity is what prevents these.

opt_null_ok.message: Not quite. A null foreign key is acceptable, but a non-null foreign key that has no matching primary key in the referenced table is not. That creates an orphan record and breaks referential integrity.

opt_duplicate.message: Not quite. This is not a duplicate-row issue. The problem is that the foreign key value (99) does not match any primary key in the customers table — that is an orphan record violating referential integrity.

opt_entity.message: Not quite. Entity integrity is about the primary key being non-null. The issue here is the foreign key value (99) having no match in the referenced table — that is a referential integrity violation.

correct.message: Right. A non-null foreign key that has no matching primary key in the referenced table creates an orphan record and breaks referential integrity.

incorrect.message: Remember: referential integrity requires that a non-null foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table.

hints: What is the term for a row whose foreign key value has no matching row in the referenced table?
A null foreign key is fine. A non-null foreign key with no match is the problem.

steps.title: Find the Foreign Key and the Orphan
steps.lede: Given the QuickShip orders and customers tables, pick the foreign key column and identify which row value would break referential integrity.

public.intro: The orders table has been modified so that one row references a customer that does not exist in the customers table. Use the table to answer the tasks below.

tasks.prompt: Select the column in the orders table that is the foreign key referencing the customers table.
Select the row that creates an orphan record — its foreign key value has no matching primary key in the customers table.
Select the specific cell containing the foreign key value that breaks referential integrity.

task_fk_column.correct: Correct. customer_id in the orders table is the foreign key — its values must match a customer_id in the customers table.
task_fk_column.incorrect: The foreign key is the column whose values reference the primary key of another table. Which column in orders points to the customers table?

task_orphan_row.correct: Correct. Order 107 has customer_id = 99, which does not exist in the customers table — making it an orphan record.
task_orphan_row.incorrect: Check each row's customer_id value. Which one does not appear in the customers table (valid customer_ids are 1–5)?

task_orphan_cell.correct: Correct. The value 99 in the customer_id column of order 107 has no matching row in the customers table, breaking referential integrity.
task_orphan_cell.incorrect: Find the row with the unmatched customer_id and select the cell in the customer_id column for that row.

correct.message: Excellent. You identified the foreign key column and pinpointed the exact cell that breaks referential integrity.

incorrect.message: The foreign key column links orders to customers. An orphan record has a foreign key value that matches no primary key in the referenced table.

hints: The foreign key is the column that references another table's primary key. Which column in orders does that?
Valid customer_ids in the customers table are 1 through 5. Which order row has a customer_id outside that range?

steps.title: One Customer, Many Orders
steps.lede: A customer can place several orders, but each order belongs to at most one customer — that asymmetry has a name.

blocks.text: A customer can place several orders, but an order relates to at most one customer. That asymmetry between customers and orders is a specific, named kind of relationship.
In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side — one department has many employees, and here, one customer has many orders.

blocks.title: One-to-many: customers (1) → orders (M)
blocks.alt_text: Two table boxes connected by a 1:M arrow. customers is the one side (customer_id PK). orders is the many side, with customer_id marked as the foreign key. The arrow points from customers to orders, showing one customer can have many orders.

blocks.text: A customer can place a minimum of zero and a maximum of many orders, while an order relates to a maximum of one customer — so orders is the many side. The foreign key customer_id is placed in the orders table and must match a valid customer_id in customers. A single customers row can't hold several order ids in one column, so the foreign key has to go on the many side.

steps.title: Telling One-to-Many from One-to-One
steps.lede: See how to decide which side is 'one' and which is 'many' by checking which side repeats the key.

segments.label: Telling one-to-one from one-to-many by checking which side repeats the key
segments.summary: Compares two pairs of tables by checking whether the key values repeat on each side. In the customers and tiers example every customer ID appears once on both sides, so the relationship is one-to-one. In the customers and orders example IDs are unique on the customers side but repeat on the orders side, because Maria placed two orders, so it is one-to-many. Flipping the sides gives many-to-one.

blocks.group_title: Reading one-to-many from repeated key values

bridge.before: Watch how the clip decides 'one' versus 'many' by looking for duplicate key values on each side. The one-to-one example is the warm-up.
bridge.after: The clip never says foreign key, never shows a customer with zero orders, and does not say an order's customer ID must match a real customer. The text above covers those and where the foreign key goes.

steps.title: Where Does the Foreign Key Go?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of which table holds the foreign key in a 1:M relationship.

public.prompt: In the QuickShip database, one customer can place many orders. Where should the foreign key (customer_id) be placed?

options.text: In the orders table — the many side holds the foreign key
In the customers table — the one side holds the foreign key
In both tables — each side needs a copy of the foreign key
In neither table — a separate linking table is always required

opt_orders.message: Correct. In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key is placed in the table on the many side — here, the orders table.

opt_customers.message: Not quite. Placing the foreign key in the customers table would require storing multiple order IDs in one customer row, which is not how relational tables work. The foreign key goes in the orders table (the many side).

opt_both.message: Not quite. Only the many side needs the foreign key. Placing it in both tables would create redundancy and inconsistency.

opt_neither.message: Not quite. A separate junction table is needed for many-to-many relationships, not one-to-many. In a 1:M relationship, the foreign key goes directly in the many-side table.

correct.message: Right. The foreign key always goes in the many-side table — here, orders holds customer_id to reference the customers table.

incorrect.message: In a one-to-many relationship, the many side holds the foreign key. Think about which table has multiple rows per entity on the other side.

hints: Which table has multiple rows for a single customer? That is the many side.
The many side holds the foreign key because each row on the many side references exactly one row on the one side.

steps.title: Identify the One Side and the Many Side
steps.lede: Given the QuickShip customers and orders tables, identify which is the one side, which is the many side, and which table holds the foreign key.

public.intro: The orders table is shown below. Customer 1 (Amara Okafor) has placed orders 101 and 103; customer 2 (Emeka Nwosu) has placed orders 102 and 106. Use the table to answer the tasks.

tasks.prompt: Select a row that shows the same customer_id appearing more than once — evidence that orders is the many side of the relationship.
Select the column in the orders table that is the foreign key linking each order to its customer.

task_many_side_evidence.correct: Correct. Order 103 also has customer_id = 1, showing that customer 1 has multiple orders — confirming orders is the many side.
task_many_side_evidence.incorrect: Look for a customer_id value that appears in more than one row. That repetition shows orders is the many side.

task_fk_in_orders.correct: Correct. customer_id in the orders table is the foreign key — it references the primary key of the customers table and is placed on the many side.
task_fk_in_orders.incorrect: The foreign key is the column that references another table's primary key. Which column in orders points to the customers table?

correct.message: Well done. You identified the many side (orders) and the foreign key column (customer_id) that links each order to its customer.

incorrect.message: The many side is the table where the same value from the other table appears in multiple rows. The foreign key is the column that creates that link.

hints: Look for a customer_id value that appears in more than one row in the orders table.
The foreign key is in the orders table because each order belongs to exactly one customer, but one customer can have many orders.

steps.title: What You've Learned
steps.lede: Two ideas to carry forward from this tile.

blocks.text: A foreign key in the child table must match an existing primary key in the parent table — or be null. A non-null value with no match is an orphan record, and referential integrity prevents these. In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key always lives on the many side: orders holds customer_id because one customer can have many orders, but an order belongs to only one customer.

blocks.title: Up Next: Normalization and Many-to-Many Relationships
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll see what happens when you store the same customer data on every order row — and how splitting tables into a normalised design, plus a junction table, solves that problem.

remediation_steps.title: Null vs. Non-Null Foreign Keys
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a null foreign key (allowed) and a non-null one with no match (orphan).

blocks.text: Order 107 with customer_id = NULL: allowed — the constraint says a null value doesn't violate referential integrity. Order 107 with customer_id = 99: not allowed if no customer with id 99 exists in the customers table — that row becomes an orphan record. The rule is: non-null foreign key values must match an existing primary key in the referenced table.

remediation_steps.title: Why the Foreign Key Goes on the Many Side
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between storing the link on the one side versus the many side.

blocks.text: If you tried to store order ids in the customers table, one customer with three orders would need three order_id columns — or a repeating group. That breaks the table structure. Instead, each order row stores one customer_id. One customer row can match many order rows, but each order row points to exactly one customer. The foreign key always goes on the many side.
